claim: The neural noise hypothesis of dyslexia posits an imbalance between excitatory and inhibitory (E/I) brain activity as an underlying mechanism of reading difficulties.
source: The neural noise hypothesis of dyslexia posits an imbalance between excitatory and inhibitory (E/I) brain activity as an underlying mechanism of reading difficulties.
evidence: This is a statement about the neural noise hypothesis cited from the literature.

claim: This study examined both EEG and MRS biomarkers of E/I balance in 120 Polish adolescents and young adults (60 with dyslexia, 60 controls).
source: This study provides the first direct test of this hypothesis using both electroencephalography (EEG) power spectrum measures in 120 Polish adolescents and young adults (60 with dyslexia, 60 controls) and glutamate (Glu) and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) concentrations from magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) at 7T MRI scanner in half of the sample.
evidence: The study design and sample size are described in the abstract.

claim: MRS measurements were obtained at 7T MRI scanner in half of the sample.
source: This study provides the first direct test of this hypothesis using both electroencephalography (EEG) power spectrum measures in 120 Polish adolescents and young adults (60 with dyslexia, 60 controls) and glutamate (Glu) and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) concentrations from magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) at 7T MRI scanner in half of the sample.
evidence: The MRS acquisition parameters are stated in the abstract.

claim: The study found no evidence of E/I balance differences between dyslexic and control groups.
source: Our results, supported by Bayesian statistics, show no evidence of E/I balance differences between groups, challenging the hypothesis that cortical hyperexcitability underlies dyslexia.
evidence: The main finding is stated in the abstract and supported by statistical analyses.

claim: The neural noise hypothesis predicts increased cortical excitation leading to more variable and less synchronous neural firing.
source: The hypothesis predicts increased cortical excitation leading to more variable and less synchronous neural firing.
evidence: This is a description of the neural noise hypothesis from the literature.

claim: Increased cortical excitation supposedly results in disrupted sensory representations and impedes phonological awareness and multisensory integration skills, crucial for learning to read.
source: This instability supposedly results in disrupted sensory representations and impedes phonological awareness and multisensory integration skills, crucial for learning to read (Hancock et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the predicted consequences of the neural noise hypothesis.

claim: Studies testing the neural noise hypothesis are lacking.

claim: E/I balance can be measured non-invasively through assessment of glutamate and GABA neurotransmitters concentration via MRS.
source: The non-invasive measurement of the E/I balance can be derived through assessment of glutamate (Glu) and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) neurotransmitters concentration via magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) (Finkelman et al., 2022) or through various E/I estimations from the electroencephalography (EEG) signal (Ahmad et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to methodological literature.

claim: E/I balance can be measured through various E/I estimations from the EEG signal.

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to methodological literature.

claim: Higher Glu concentrations in the midline occipital cortex correlated with poorer reading performance in children.

evidence: This is a summary of findings from previous studies.

evidence: This is a summary of findings from previous studies.

evidence: This is a summary of findings from previous studies.
